title: The Hidden Patterns
subtitle: Spirals, symmetry, chance, infinity and the primes that run the world
subject: Maths

pages.h: The rabbit problem
p: In 1202 an Italian mathematician known as Fibonacci published a puzzle. Start with one pair of baby rabbits. Each pair takes a month to grow up, then produces a new pair every month forever. How many pairs do you have after a year?

Count it out. Month one: 1 pair. Month two: still 1, they are growing up. Month three: 2. Then 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, 89, 144. After twelve months: 144 pairs, or 377 if, like Fibonacci, you let the first pair breed straight away. Each number is the sum of the two before it. That is the whole rule, and the list is called the Fibonacci sequence.

The rabbits are nonsense, of course. Real rabbits die, and the sexes do not come out in tidy pairs. But the sequence turned out to be anything but nonsense. It had already been described by Indian scholars studying poetry rhythms centuries earlier, and it keeps turning up in places that have nothing to do with rabbits.

Here is the first surprise. Divide any Fibonacci number by the one before it. 8 divided by 5 is 1.6. 13 divided by 8 is 1.625. 55 divided by 34 is 1.6176. The further you go, the closer the answer creeps to one particular number: 1.6180339887 and on without end. Mathematicians call it phi, or the golden ratio. It is about to show up in a sunflower.
pages.cap: Squares with Fibonacci side lengths fit together into a spiral that grows but never changes shape.
pages.fact: Did you know? Fibonacci's real name was Leonardo of Pisa. The nickname was given to him 600 years after he died.

pages.h: Why a sunflower counts in Fibonacci
p: Look closely at the centre of a sunflower. The seeds form two sets of spirals, one curling clockwise and one counterclockwise. Count them. On a typical flower you will find 34 one way and 55 the other. On a big one, 55 and 89. Pine cones give 8 and 13. A pineapple gives 8, 13 and 21. These are Fibonacci numbers, almost every time.

The plant is not counting. It is solving a packing problem. New seeds form at the centre and push older ones outward. The plant places each new seed at a fixed angle from the last one. If that angle were a simple fraction of a turn, such as a half or a quarter, the seeds would line up in straight rows with wasted gaps between. The angle that packs seeds most evenly, with no rows and no gaps, is about 137.5 degrees, called the golden angle, because it divides the circle in the golden ratio. Spirals built from that angle automatically come out in Fibonacci numbers.

Is this really everywhere, or do people just see what they want to see? In 2016 a citizen science project in Manchester counted the spirals on 657 sunflowers. About three in four followed Fibonacci exactly. The rest were close relatives, or simply messy. Nature follows the rule often, not always, and the exceptions are now studied as carefully as the rule.
pages.cap: Seeds placed 137.5 degrees apart pack with no gaps and no straight rows. Count the spirals: 34 and 55.

pages.h: The golden ratio, the honest version
p: The golden ratio, 1.618, has a simple definition. Cut a line into a long piece and a short piece so that the whole line divided by the long piece equals the long piece divided by the short piece. There is only one way to do it, and the answer is phi. A rectangle whose sides are in that ratio is a golden rectangle. Cut a square off one end and the leftover is another golden rectangle, forever.

Now the warning. You will read that the Parthenon in Athens, the Great Pyramid, famous paintings and the human face are all built on the golden ratio. Most of these claims fall apart when you measure. The Parthenon fits only if you choose where to draw the lines. A nautilus shell is a true spiral that grows at a constant rate, but it grows by about 3 times per turn, not the 6.9 times a golden spiral would need. Studies that ask people to pick the most pleasing rectangle find no strong preference for the golden one.

Why does the myth persist? Because phi really does appear in plants, in some crystals and throughout mathematics, and because 1.618 is a satisfying number to find. The lesson is one that runs through this whole book. Patterns are real, and pattern-hunting is powerful. But the same brain that finds true patterns will happily invent false ones. The difference is measurement.
pages.cap: Many shapes are called golden. Measure before you believe it. The pentagon genuinely hides phi in its diagonals.

pages.h: A spiral galaxy, a hurricane and a snail shell all follow the same kind of curve
p: It is called a logarithmic spiral: it gets bigger with every turn but never changes shape. Zoom in or out and it looks the same. Falcons dive along one to keep their prey in view. It appears wherever something grows while keeping its proportions.

pages.q: The Fibonacci sequence runs 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. What comes next?
pages.why: Each number is the sum of the two before it. 8 plus 13 is 21.

pages.h: Symmetry: what stays the same when you move
p: A butterfly is symmetrical: flip it over an imaginary line down the middle and it looks the same. That is mirror symmetry, and it is only one kind. A starfish has rotation symmetry: turn it one fifth of a circle and it looks unchanged. A row of fence posts has translation symmetry: slide it along one post and nothing has changed. Mathematicians define symmetry as any move you can make to an object that leaves it looking exactly as it did before.

Why do living things bother? Mirror symmetry comes almost free for anything that moves in a straight line, because left and right face the same world. Most animals that walk, swim or fly have it. Animals that sit still and wait for food from all directions, like sea anemones and starfish, tend to be round and have rotation symmetry instead. Plants, which cannot move at all, are often symmetrical around their stem.

Symmetry also signals health. A face or a body that grew evenly, without disease or injury, comes out more symmetrical, and across many species, from barn swallows to humans, animals prefer symmetrical mates.

Physicists take it further. The deepest laws of nature are statements of symmetry: the rules of physics are the same here as on the other side of the galaxy, and the same today as a billion years ago.
pages.cap: A mirror line down the middle. Flip the butterfly across it and nothing changes. That is a symmetry.

pages.h: Why every snowflake has six arms
p: Catch a snowflake on a dark sleeve and look. Six arms, every time. Never five, never seven. The explanation is sitting in a water molecule.

Each water molecule is a V shape, with the two hydrogen atoms at an angle of 104.5 degrees. When water freezes, the molecules link up through weak hydrogen bonds, and the only way the V shapes can fit together neatly is in a hexagonal pattern, like a honeycomb. A snowflake is just that hexagonal lattice grown large enough to see. The six-fold symmetry of a crystal you can hold comes from the angle of a molecule a billion times smaller.

Why are no two alike? A snowflake grows as it falls through air that is constantly changing in temperature and humidity. Each small change makes the arms grow in a slightly different way: long and thin, or flat and plate-like, or branching. The six arms stay matched because they all pass through the same air at the same moment. But the sequence of conditions a flake meets on its 1-kilometre fall is never repeated. A single flake contains about 10 billion billion molecules.

In 1611 the astronomer Johannes Kepler wrote a small book asking exactly this question: why six? He guessed it had to do with how tiny balls pack together. He was close. It took 300 years and the discovery of atoms to finish his answer.
pages.cap: Frozen water molecules lock into hexagons. Every snowflake inherits the six-sided shape of that lattice.

pages.h: Wallpaper: there are only 17 ways
p: Imagine designing a repeating pattern to cover a wall or a floor: tiles, wallpaper, fabric. You can choose any shapes and colours you like. But underneath the decoration, the pattern must repeat by some combination of slides, turns, mirrors and glides. How many fundamentally different ways are there to do that?

Exactly 17. Not roughly, not usually: exactly. This was proved in 1891 by a Russian crystallographer named Evgraf Fedorov. Every repeating flat pattern ever made, from ancient Egyptian tiles to a modern phone case, belongs to one of 17 types, and no artist will ever invent an eighteenth. The maths forbids it.

Artists found most of them long before mathematicians counted. The Alhambra palace in Granada, Spain, decorated by Islamic craftsmen in the 1300s, contains tilings from at least 13 of the 17 groups, and some scholars argue all 17 are there. The craftsmen had no theory. They had centuries of experiment and a sharp sense of what could be made to fit.

Step into three dimensions and the count rises to 230 ways for crystals to repeat. Every mineral, every metal, every grain of salt is built on one of those 230. Chemists use the list to work out the structure of a new crystal from the way it scatters X-rays. A limit discovered for wallpaper turned out to describe the inside of every solid on Earth.
pages.cap: The tiled walls of medieval palaces explored the 17 wallpaper patterns centuries before anyone proved there were 17.
pages.fact: Did you know? A regular pentagon cannot tile a floor on its own. Triangles, squares and hexagons are the only regular shapes that can.

pages.h: The tile that never repeats
p: Squares tile a floor in a pattern that repeats. So do hexagons. For centuries mathematicians wondered: is there a single tile shape that can cover a floor completely, with no gaps, but can never be arranged in a repeating pattern, no matter how hard you try?

In 1974 the physicist Roger Penrose found a pair of tiles, a kite and a dart, that together do this. Lay them by his rules and the pattern goes on forever without ever repeating. Beautiful, but it took two shapes. The hunt for a single such tile, nicknamed an 'einstein' from the German for one stone, went on for 50 years.

In November 2022 a retired printing technician in England named David Smith, who played with shapes as a hobby, cut out a 13-sided shape that looked like a hat and could not make it repeat. He contacted mathematicians, and in March 2023 they proved it: the hat tiles the plane, and only in non-repeating ways. One catch: roughly one hat in eight has to be flipped over. By May the same team found a second shape, the spectre, that works without any flipping at all.

A hobbyist with cardboard and scissors solved a problem that had defeated professionals for half a century. Mathematics is one of the few fields where that still happens, because the only equipment you need is an idea.
pages.cap: Squares and hexagons repeat. The hat, found in 2022, covers a floor but never repeats, no matter how you lay it.

pages.h: Try it: a six-fold paper snowflake
p: Most paper snowflakes have four or eight arms, which real snow never does. Here is how to fold for six, like nature.
steps: Start with a square sheet of thin paper. Fold it in half diagonally to make a triangle, then in half again to make a smaller triangle.

Hold the triangle with the right-angle corner pointing down. You now need to fold it into thirds, not halves. Fold the left corner across so its edge lines up one third of the way over, then fold the right corner across on top. Adjust until the three layers match. This is the step people get wrong; take your time.
Cut off the ragged top points so the edge is straight.
Cut shapes into the two long edges: triangles, curves, little notches. Leave the folded tip intact or the flake falls apart.
Unfold carefully. You should see six identical arms. Every cut you made appears six times.
Make a second flake with different cuts. Just as in nature, it is impossible to get two the same.
pages.cap: Fold into sixths and every snip appears six times. The symmetry of the fold decides the symmetry of the flake.
pages.safe: Use blunt-tipped scissors and cut away from your fingers.

pages.h: The coin does not remember
p: Flip a fair coin and get heads five times in a row. What are the chances the next one is tails? Most people feel that tails is 'due'. It is not. The chance is exactly one half, as it was for every flip. The coin has no memory. It has not noticed the last five flips and feels no pressure to even things out.
This mistake is so common it has a name: the gambler's fallacy. A family with four daughters is no more likely to have a son next. A basketball player who has missed three shots is not owed a basket.

Long runs are normal. Flip a coin 100 times and you are more likely than not to see a run of at least six heads or six tails somewhere. If someone shows you 100 made-up flips, you can often spot the fake because people do not put in enough long runs.

Is a coin actually fair? In 2023 a team of 48 researchers flipped coins 350,757 times and found a tiny bias: the coin landed the same way up as it started about 50.8 percent of the time, because of a slight wobble in the air. So a coin does remember one thing, which side started on top. Across a long series of flips, though, heads and tails come out even, and the next flip is still a toss-up.
pages.cap: Heads or tails, it is one half every time. The coin does not know what happened before.
pages.fact: Did you know? The chance of ten heads in a row is 1 in 1,024. Try it a thousand times and you will probably see it.

pages.h: Dice, and why the casino always wins
p: Roll two dice and add them up. There are 36 equally likely ways the dice can land. Only one makes 2: a 1 and a 1. Only one makes 12. But six different ways make 7: 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4, 4 and 3, 5 and 2, 6 and 1. So 7 comes up one roll in six, and 2 comes up only one roll in 36.

Casinos use that counting to make certain of winning. Take European roulette. The wheel has 37 pockets: 18 red, 18 black and one green zero. Bet on red and you have 18 chances in 37, which is 48.6 percent, not 50. The green pocket is the house's edge. For every 100 dollars bet on red, over time, the casino keeps about 2.70. On an American wheel with two green pockets, it keeps 5.26.

In the short run anyone can win, which is what keeps people playing. But the maths does not care about the short run. A casino hosting a million bets a night is as sure of its profit as a shop is of its sales. It is running an arithmetic problem with a known answer.
The same tool, counting the ways, is how insurance companies set prices, how weather forecasters say 70 percent chance of rain, and how doctors decide whether a test result means anything.
pages.cap: Two dice, 36 ways to land. Six of them add to 7, so 7 is the most common total by far.

pages.h: The birthday surprise
p: How many people do you need in a room before it is more likely than not that two of them share a birthday? Most people guess around 180, half of 365. The real answer is 23. In a class of 23 students the chance of a shared birthday is 50.7 percent. With 50 people it is 97 percent. With 70, it is 99.9 percent.

That feels wrong, and the reason it feels wrong is the key. You are probably imagining whether someone shares your birthday. That is unlikely with 23 people, about 6 percent. But the question is whether any two people share one, and that means every pair counts. In a room of 23 there are 253 different pairs. Each pair has about a 1 in 365 chance of matching, and 253 chances at 1 in 365 add up fast.

Here is a way to see it. The first person can have any birthday. The second must avoid one date: 364 chances in 365. The third must avoid two: 363 in 365. Multiply those shrinking fractions together for 23 people and the chance that nobody matches drops below one half.

The birthday problem shows up in computer security, where it sets how long a digital fingerprint must be before two files could accidentally share one. It also explains why coincidences are so common. With enough pairs, something always matches.
pages.cap: Six children, fifteen pairs. In a room of 23 there are 253 pairs, enough that two birthdays probably match.

pages.q: A fair coin has landed heads six times in a row. What is the chance that the next flip is tails?
opts: More than half, because tails is due
Less than half, because the coin is on a heads streak
pages.why: Each flip is independent. The coin has no memory of earlier results, so the chance stays one half.

pages.h: Why one-in-a-million things happen every day
p: Every so often the news reports someone who won a lottery twice, or a person who dreamed of a plane crash the night before one happened. People call these miracles. Mathematicians call them Tuesday.

Here is why. About 8 billion people are alive. Suppose each of them experiences a few hundred small events a day. That is more than a trillion events every day worldwide. An event that has a one in a million chance of happening to any given person on any given day will happen to about 8,000 people a day. It is rare for you. It is routine for the world. A mathematician named John Littlewood put it this way: you should expect a one-in-a-million event about once a month.

Now the lottery. In Canada's Lotto 6/49, the chance of matching all six numbers with one ticket is 1 in 13,983,816. For Lotto Max it is 1 in 33,294,800. You are far more likely to be struck by lightning in your lifetime, roughly 1 in 15,000 in Canada. Yet someone wins most weeks, because millions of tickets are sold. Someone winning is almost certain. You winning is almost impossible. Both are true at once.
The people who dreamed of a crash and saw none the next day do not call the newspaper. Only the hit gets counted. Keep asking what you are not being shown, and most miracles shrink to arithmetic.
pages.cap: Millions of people, millions of small events a day. Something astonishing is happening to somebody right now, by chance.

pages.h: How to read a graph without being fooled
p: A graph is a picture of numbers, and pictures can lie while every number in them is true. Three tricks cover most of the damage.
First, the chopped axis. A bar chart where the vertical axis starts at 95 instead of 0 can make a rise from 96 to 98 look like a doubling. Always check where the axis begins.

Second, the average that hides the picture. If nine people earn 30,000 dollars and one earns 3 million, the average income is 327,000 dollars, and nobody in the room earns anything like it. The median, the middle value when you line everyone up, is 30,000, and tells the truth. Ask which one you are being shown.

Third, and biggest: correlation is not causation. In most cities, months with high ice cream sales also have more drownings. Ice cream does not cause drowning. Hot weather causes both. Two things rising together may be linked, or both may be driven by a third thing, or it may be a coincidence. A famous website collects these: the number of films Nicolas Cage appears in each year tracked the number of people who drowned in swimming pools for a decade. Nobody thinks one caused the other.
When someone shows you a graph to persuade you, that is the moment to slow down and ask where the zero is, what kind of average it uses, and what else could explain the shape.
pages.cap: Ice cream sales rise in summer. So do swims and drownings. The heat drives both; neither causes the other.

pages.h: A million, a billion, a trillion
p: The words sound similar, so people treat them as roughly similar sizes. They are not. A million is a thousand thousands. A billion is a thousand millions. A trillion is a thousand billions. Each step is a thousand times bigger, and the human brain is terrible at feeling what that means.

Try time. A million seconds is about 11 and a half days. A billion seconds is about 31.7 years. A trillion seconds is about 31,700 years, which takes you back before farming, before writing, to the last ice age. If you had a million dollars and spent 1,000 dollars a day, you would run out in under three years. With a billion, you would last 2,700 years.

Try distance. A million millimetres is a kilometre, a 12-minute walk. A billion millimetres is 1,000 kilometres, Toronto to Quebec City and a bit more. A trillion millimetres would wrap around the Earth 25 times.

Now the big ones. There are about 7.5 billion billion grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth, written as 7.5 followed by 18 zeros. There are more stars in the observable universe than that: roughly 10 followed by 22 zeros, or more. And there are about 7 followed by 27 zeros atoms in your body, far more atoms in you than there are stars in the sky.
pages.cap: A million seconds is 11 days. A billion seconds is 31 years. The clock is the easiest way to feel the gap.
pages.fact: Did you know? Nobody has ever counted to a billion out loud. At one number per second with no sleep it would take 31 years.

pages.h: Doubling: the chessboard and the Moon
p: An old story tells of an inventor who showed a king the game of chess. The king offered any reward. The inventor asked for a single grain of rice on the first square of the board, two on the second, four on the third, and so on, doubling each time for all 64 squares. The king laughed and agreed.

Square 20 holds about half a million. Square 30: half a billion. Square 40: half a trillion. By the last square the pile is 9 billion billion grains, and the whole board holds 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 grains. That is roughly 460 billion tonnes of rice, close to 900 years of today's entire world harvest.

This is exponential growth: when something grows by a fixed percentage of what is already there. It starts slowly and then explodes. A piece of paper 0.1 millimetres thick, folded in half 42 times, would be thick enough to reach the Moon. Nobody can fold paper that many times, because the stack gets too thick to bend, but 42 doublings of a tenth of a millimetre is 440,000 kilometres.

Exponential growth is why a bacterial infection can go from harmless to dangerous in a day, why a virus that each person passes to two others swamps hospitals in weeks. If you remember one pattern from this book for the rest of your life, make it this one.
pages.cap: The first five squares look harmless. Square 64 holds more rice than the world grows in 900 years.

pages.h: There are more ways to shuffle a deck of cards than there are atoms on Earth
p: Fifty-two cards can be arranged in about 8 followed by 67 zeros ways. Earth contains about 1 followed by 50 zeros atoms. Shuffle a deck well and you almost certainly hold an order no human has ever held before.

pages.q: A pond weed doubles the area it covers every day and fills the whole pond on day 30. On which day did it cover half the pond?
pages.why: If it doubles daily and is full on day 30, it must have been half full the day before. Exponential growth looks slow until the very end.

pages.h: Infinity is not a number
p: Infinity is not the biggest number. There is no biggest number, because whatever you name, adding one gives a bigger one. Infinity is better thought of as a description: a process that never stops. The counting numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on go on forever, and we say there are infinitely many.

Infinity behaves badly if you treat it like an ordinary number. The mathematician David Hilbert imagined a hotel with infinitely many rooms, all full. A new guest arrives. No problem: ask every guest to move up one room. Room 1 moves to 2, room 2 moves to 3, and so on. Everyone still has a room and room 1 is now free. Infinitely many new guests arrive. Still no problem: ask every guest to move to double their room number. Now all the odd rooms are empty, and there are infinitely many of them.

Here is the strangest consequence. There are as many even numbers as there are whole numbers. That sounds absurd, since the even numbers are only half of them. But pair them up: 1 with 2, 2 with 4, 3 with 6, and so on. Every whole number gets exactly one even partner and nothing is left over on either side. When two collections can be perfectly paired, mathematicians say they are the same size. A part of infinity can be as big as the whole.
pages.cap: Hop by twos forever and you still have as many landing spots as there are whole numbers. Infinity does not run out.

pages.h: Some infinities are bigger than others
p: In the 1870s a German mathematician named Georg Cantor asked a question nobody had dared: can one infinity be bigger than another? Everyone assumed infinity was simply infinity. Cantor proved them wrong.

He considered the counting numbers, 1, 2, 3 and so on, and then all the decimals between 0 and 1, like 0.5, 0.333..., 0.7071... Suppose you could list every one of those decimals, matched to the counting numbers: a first decimal, a second, a third, forever. Cantor showed how to build a new decimal that is not on the list. Take the first digit of the first decimal and change it. Take the second digit of the second and change it. Keep going down the diagonal. The number you build differs from every number on the list in at least one place. So the list was never complete. The decimals cannot be paired with the counting numbers. There are more of them. Infinitely more.
Cantor's proof fits on a page. It was also hated. Leading mathematicians called it a disease. Cantor spent years fighting for it and suffered badly.

It left a question Cantor could not answer: is there an infinity between the counting numbers and the decimals? In 1963 it was proved that the question cannot be settled from the usual rules of mathematics at all. It is neither true nor false. Mathematicians argue to this day about what that means.
pages.cap: Between any two decimals there are infinitely more. The decimals form a bigger infinity than the counting numbers.

pages.h: Primes: the atoms of arithmetic
p: A prime is a whole number bigger than 1 that can be divided evenly only by 1 and itself. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23. Anything else is composite: it can be broken into smaller factors. 12 is 2 times 2 times 3.

Primes matter because every whole number is built from them in exactly one way. 60 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 5, and there is no other set of primes that multiplies to 60. This is called the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, and it makes primes the atoms of numbers: the pieces that cannot be split, from which everything else is made, in only one recipe each.

Do the primes ever run out? Around 300 BC the Greek mathematician Euclid proved they do not. Suppose you had a complete list of all the primes. Multiply them all together and add 1. The new number is not divisible by any prime on your list, because each one leaves a remainder of 1. So either the new number is itself a prime you missed, or it is built from primes you missed. Either way, the list was not complete. No list ever can be. There are infinitely many primes.
Yet they are scattered without any pattern anyone has found. Predicting exactly where the next prime falls is one of the oldest unsolved problems in mathematics.
pages.cap: Every number is built from primes the way every molecule is built from atoms, and in only one way.
pages.fact: Did you know? 2 is the only even prime. Every other even number can be divided by 2.

pages.h: The hunt for giant primes
p: How big is the biggest prime anyone knows? As this book was written, the record was a number with 41,024,320 digits. Printed in a normal book font, it would fill about 12,000 pages. It was found on 12 October 2024 by Luke Durant, a researcher who rented thousands of graphics processors in data centres across 17 countries to search.

The number is written as 2 to the power of 136,279,841, minus 1. Primes of this form, one less than a power of two, are called Mersenne primes, and they are easier to test than ordinary numbers of the same size. Only 52 of them have ever been found. Since 1996 almost every record has come from a volunteer project called GIMPS, where ordinary people donate their computer's spare time.

Why bother? Partly because the test is a brutal workout for computer hardware, and it has exposed flaws in processors. Partly because searching for structure in the primes has, over and over, led to mathematics that turned out to be useful decades later. And partly because people climb mountains.

The 41-million-digit record will fall. Nobody can say when. There is no formula that produces primes, and no shortcut that says where the next Mersenne prime hides. Finding one is like searching a desert for a particular grain of sand, except that the desert is infinite and the grains get farther apart the further you walk.
pages.cap: Computers test numbers in binary. The largest known prime is a string of 136,279,841 ones, with no zeros.

pages.h: Primes keep your secrets
p: Every time you buy something online, send a private message or log into a bank, prime numbers are protecting you. The trick depends on a strange imbalance in arithmetic.

Multiplying two primes together is easy. A computer can multiply two 300-digit primes in a fraction of a second. Going backwards, taking the 600-digit result and finding which two primes made it, is brutally hard. With the best known methods and every computer on Earth, cracking a well-chosen 600-digit product would take longer than the age of the universe.

The system called RSA, invented in 1977, uses that gap. Your bank publishes the big product openly, as a lock anyone can use to scramble a message. Only the bank knows the two primes, which are the key that unscrambles it. Anyone can see the lock. Nobody can work out the key in time to matter.

There is a cloud on the horizon. In 1994 a mathematician named Peter Shor showed that a quantum computer, if a big enough one could be built, would factor huge numbers quickly and break RSA. No such machine exists yet, and experts argue about whether it is 10 years away or 50. In 2024 the United States published new encryption standards built on different mathematics, designed to survive quantum computers, and governments and companies are already switching. A problem about the atoms of arithmetic has become a matter of national security.
pages.cap: Your phone and a shop's server agree on a secret using primes. Anyone listening gets only the product, not the factors.

pages.h: Try it: the sieve of Eratosthenes
p: A Greek librarian found a way to catch every prime up to 100 with nothing but crossing out. It still works and takes ten minutes.
steps: Write the numbers 1 to 100 in a grid, ten per row.
Cross out 1. It is not a prime.
Circle 2, the first prime. Then cross out every multiple of 2: 4, 6, 8 and so on. Half the grid is gone.
Find the next number not crossed out, which is 3. Circle it and cross out every multiple of 3 that is still standing: 9, 15, 21, and so on.
Repeat with 5, then 7. After 7 you can stop, because any composite number under 100 must have a factor of 7 or less.
Everything still standing is prime. You should have exactly 25 circled numbers. Look at how unevenly they are spread, and notice the pairs that differ by 2, like 11 and 13 or 71 and 73.
pages.cap: Hop along the number line by threes and cross out every landing place. Do it for 2, 3, 5 and 7, and only primes survive.

pages.q: Why is it hard to crack the lock in RSA encryption?
opts: Multiplying two big primes is easy but finding them again from the product is extremely slow
pages.why: The product is public. Security rests on the fact that no known fast method can split a huge number back into its two prime factors.

pages.h: The insects that count in primes
p: In the eastern United States live cicadas that spend 13 or 17 years underground as grubs. Then, all at once, billions of them tunnel out in the same few weeks, sing deafeningly, mate, lay eggs and die. The forest goes quiet for another 13 or 17 years.

Why those numbers? Both are primes, and that may be the point. Suppose a predator, say a bird or a wasp, had a population that boomed every 4 years. A cicada that emerged every 12 years would meet the boom every single time, because 12 is divisible by 4. A cicada that emerged every 13 years would meet a 4-year boom only every 52 years, and a 6-year boom only every 78. A prime cycle slips through the gaps in every shorter cycle. Biologists argue about whether predators really drove this or whether the prime cycles help the broods avoid interbreeding, but the arithmetic works either way.

In spring 2024 something rare happened. A 13-year brood and a 17-year brood emerged in the same season, their ranges touching in Illinois. The last time those two broods coincided was 1803. The next time will be 2245. That is 13 times 17, which is 221 years, exactly as the primes predict.
Cicadas cannot do arithmetic. But over millions of years, the ones that happened to use prime cycles outlasted the ones that did not, and arithmetic did the rest.
pages.cap: Thirteen or seventeen summers pass. Then, for a few weeks, the trees are full of cicadas, and then silence again.

pages.h: Honeycomb: the cheapest way to hold honey
p: Bees build their comb from wax, and wax is expensive. It takes about 8 grams of honey to make 1 gram of wax. So a hive that wastes wax wastes food. Suppose you want to divide a flat surface into equal cells, with no gaps, using the least possible wall. What shape should the cells be?

Only three regular shapes tile a flat surface with no gaps: triangles, squares and hexagons. For the same area, a hexagon has a shorter perimeter than a square or triangle, so it uses less wall. In 36 BC the Roman writer Varro suggested that this is why bees use hexagons. Proving that no shape at all, regular or irregular, could beat the hexagon turned out to be hard. The proof was finished in 1999 by Thomas Hales.

How do bees do it? Scientists argue. One view is that bees shape each cell precisely. Another, backed by a 2013 study, is that bees build round cells and the warm wax, softened by their body heat, flows into hexagons on its own. The bee may be providing the heat, and physics the geometry.

Hexagons appear wherever space is tight: in the eyes of insects, in basalt columns where lava cooled, in the cells of a wasp's nest, and in the mirrors of the James Webb Space Telescope, which has 18 of them.
pages.cap: Hexagonal cells use the least wax for the most honey. A proof that nothing beats them took until 1999.

pages.h: How long is the coast of Canada?
p: Canada has the longest coastline in the world, usually given as about 243,000 kilometres. But ask a different question: how did anyone measure that? Measure the coast with a ruler 100 kilometres long and you skip every bay. Use a 1-kilometre ruler and the bays appear, and the length grows. Use a 1-metre ruler and every rock adds length. The coastline gets longer, without limit, the more closely you look.

A mathematician named Benoit Mandelbrot made this famous in 1967 with a paper titled 'How long is the coast of Britain?' A coastline is not a smooth curve. It is rough at every scale, and he coined a word for shapes like that: fractal.

Fractals are everywhere. A head of broccoli is made of smaller heads of broccoli, each made of smaller ones. A tree branches into branches that branch into branches. A river system looks the same from a satellite as a stream does from a bridge. Your lungs are a fractal: airways split into airways 23 times over, so that an organ that fits in your chest has a surface area of about 70 square metres, roughly a badminton court, for taking in oxygen.

Mandelbrot gave fractals a number: a dimension between a line and a surface. A smooth coast is dimension 1. Britain's is about 1.25. Norway's wrinkled fjords are about 1.5. Roughness, it turns out, can be measured.
pages.cap: Airways branch 23 times. A fractal is how 70 square metres of surface fits inside a chest.

pages.h: Why music has 12 notes
p: Pluck a guitar string. Now press it exactly halfway and pluck again. The note is the same, but higher: an octave up. Halving the string doubles the vibration rate. The A above middle C vibrates 440 times a second; the A above that, 880. Our ears hear doubled frequencies as 'the same note'.

Around 500 BC, followers of Pythagoras found that other pleasant pairs come from simple ratios too. Press the string two thirds of the way and you get a fifth, the interval that opens many famous tunes, with a frequency ratio of 3 to 2. Three quarters gives a fourth, 4 to 3. Simple ratios sound sweet. Complicated ratios sound harsh.

Here is the problem. Try to build a scale by stacking fifths: multiply by 3/2 twelve times. You land very close to seven octaves, but not exactly: 129.7 instead of 128. The gap is called the Pythagorean comma. There is no way to make pure fifths and pure octaves agree, ever. Western music solved it in the 1700s by tuning all twelve notes slightly off, splitting the error evenly, so that every key is equally and very slightly out of tune. Your piano is a compromise with arithmetic.
Twelve notes is not the only answer. Some traditions use 5, 7, 22 or 24. But 12 is where the maths comes closest to working.
pages.cap: Half the string, double the frequency. Our ears hear a doubling as the same note, one octave higher.

pages.h: The same equation describes a swinging pendulum, a plucked string and a planet's wobble
p: Anything that is pushed back toward the middle the farther it strays will swing, and all such swings obey one formula. Clocks, music, radio, the tides, the atoms in a crystal: one piece of mathematics, learned once, used everywhere.

pages.h: The maths in a zebra's stripes
p: In 1952 the mathematician Alan Turing published a paper on a very different subject: how does a plain ball of cells grow into an animal with spots or stripes? His answer used two chemicals spreading through tissue. One switches on colour and also makes more of itself. The other switches colour off and spreads faster. Where the two compete, the result is not a flat mix but a pattern: spots, stripes or blotches, depending on the numbers.

The maths predicted something testable. A tapering shape should carry stripes that split into spots as it narrows, which is exactly what you see on a cheetah's tail. A small embryo should give stripes, a bigger one spots.

For 40 years it was a pretty idea with no proof. Then in 1995 two Japanese researchers watched the stripes on growing angelfish. As the fish grew, new stripes slid in between old ones exactly as Turing's equations said they should. Since then the same mechanism has been found shaping the ridges on the roof of a mouse's mouth, the spacing of hair follicles, and the fingers of a developing hand.

Zebras are still argued over. The pattern may be Turing's, but why have stripes at all? The leading answer, supported by field experiments since 2014, is that stripes confuse biting flies. A mathematician found the how. Biologists are still working on the why.
pages.cap: Stripes on a fish follow Turing's equations. As the fish grows, new stripes slide in between the old ones.

pages.h: Why does maths work on the world?
p: Here is the deepest question in this book, and nobody has answered it. Why should a pattern worked out with pencil and paper describe the orbit of a planet, or the stripes on a fish?

In 1960 the physicist Eugene Wigner wrote an essay calling this 'the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics'. Again and again, mathematicians have invented ideas purely for their own beauty, with no use in mind, and decades or centuries later physicists have found that those exact ideas were what the universe was using all along.

Two camps argue about why. One says maths is discovered: the patterns exist out there whether or not anyone finds them, and we are explorers. The other says maths is invented: it is a language our brains built, and it fits the world because our brains evolved in the world. There is no experiment that can settle this, and mathematicians have been debating it for a very long time.

What is not in doubt is how much remains unknown. Is every even number above 2 the sum of two primes? Checked to 4 billion billion, never proved. Does the Riemann hypothesis, about where primes hide, hold? A million-dollar prize has waited since 2000. Start with any number; halve it if even, triple it and add one if odd; do you always reach 1? Nobody knows. A child could understand the question. Nobody alive can answer it.
pages.cap: Galileo wrote that the universe is written in the language of mathematics. Why that should be so is still an open question.

qs: Is mathematics discovered, like a new continent, or invented, like a language? What would change about how you see the world if one or the other were true?
The golden ratio is real in sunflowers and mostly a myth in architecture. How would you check a 'pattern in nature' claim before believing it?
A casino always wins in the long run, and so does an insurance company. Is it fair to sell people a game you know they will lose? Does it matter whether they understand the maths?
